title: Why "password123" gets cracked instantly
description: Attackers don't guess your password one letter at a time. They try the passwords everyone else already uses. Here's why length beats cleverness.

scenes.big: Your password is already on a list
scenes.say: If your password is password one two three, it's not being guessed. It's being looked up.
Billions of real passwords have leaked in data breaches. Attackers turn them into wordlists, sorted by how common they are.

steps: Swap letters: a to @, o to 0
scenes.say: A dictionary attack tries the most common passwords first, then the tweaks people think are clever. Adding a one, an exclamation mark, or swapping an o for a zero barely slows it down.

scenes.sub: four random words beat one 'clever' word
scenes.say: What actually works is length and randomness. Four random words, like 'purple kettle orbit sandwich', are far harder to crack than one word with symbols.
So: use a unique passphrase for every site, let a password manager remember them, and turn on two factor authentication. Follow for one threat explained every day.
